Notes · Unreal Engine

Motion matching on a mobile build

Aether Architect was the project I learned Unreal on, which means I did the sensible thing and started with the least sensible feature: motion matching, on an Android target. These are the notes I wish I had at the start — what the four assets actually do, and where the cost lands.

The problem motion matching solves

A hand-built blend tree is a set of decisions you make in advance: walk speed above this, play that; turn faster than this, play a pivot. It works until the character does something you did not imagine when you built the graph — and then it slides, pops, or plays a pivot that has nothing to do with where the player is going.

Motion matching inverts it. Instead of choosing animations by rule, you feed the system a database of motion-captured poses and ask, every frame, which pose in that database best matches where the character is and where the player is pushing. No transition graph. The quality of the result is the quality of your database, not the cleverness of your graph.

Four assets, one pipeline

In Unreal 5.8 the feature is spread across four pieces that are easy to confuse, because three of them are named something other than what they do.

  • PoseSearch database — the animation data, indexed. This is the thing that gets big. Every frame of every clip you include is a candidate pose, and the search runs against that set continuously.
  • MotionTrajectory — the character's intent, expressed as a short arc of predicted positions ahead of it. Not where the character is: where it is about to be. This is what the search is actually matching against, which is why a badly authored trajectory produces a character that looks like it is guessing.
  • Chooser — the selection layer. When several databases or several animation sets could apply, the Chooser picks between them. Think of it as the replacement for the top of your old state machine.
  • Animation Locomotion Library — the plumbing that connects the chosen pose to the character's movement component, so the animation drives the capsule rather than the other way round.

Once that clicked, the workflow stopped being "build a graph" and became "curate a database and describe intent". The work moved earlier, into what I captured and how I tagged it.

Where the cost actually lands

The assumption is that motion matching is expensive because the search is expensive. In a small project the search is not the problem — the database is. It sits in memory, it is read every frame, and on a phone both of those are real constraints rather than footnotes.

What helped, in order of how much it helped:

  • Cut the database before you tune the search. Every clip you include for a situation that never occurs is a permanent cost for a pose the character will never need.
  • Trim the trajectory prediction distance. A longer arc gives the system more to match on, and it also means the character commits to a turn earlier. On a touchscreen with a thumbstick that overshoots, that reads as sluggishness, not as quality.
  • Keep the Chooser small. It is tempting to add a branch for every situation. Each branch is another asset to load and another thing to debug when the character picks the wrong one.

Motion warping, and why it matters more than it sounds

Motion warping is the smaller feature that changes how the game feels. You declare a target — the lip of a ledge, the centre of a gap — and the animation is warped at runtime so the character's feet land where the target is, instead of where the clip assumed.

In a level built from floating islands with gaps you cannot walk across, that is the difference between traversal that reads as deliberate and traversal that reads as the character skating over the geometry. It is also cheap: no extra animation, no extra state, one target component per action.

StateTree instead of blueprint branches

The gameplay side of the project is written as a StateTree rather than as a blueprint graph. A state tree makes the states explicit — idle, collecting, gated, transitioning — and the transitions between them are visible as edges rather than as conditions scattered across branches. When something goes wrong, the debugger tells you which state you are in, which is more than a blueprint tangle will do for you.

What I would do differently

I would capture the database with the phone in mind from the first session, not the last. The temptation is to build the animation set you would build for a console character and then optimise it down; the result is a database that has been squeezed rather than designed, and it shows in the transitions that had to be cut.

I would also decide the camera before the locomotion. The trajectory is relative to the character and the camera, so a camera change late in the project quietly invalidates the tuning you did around it.

The project

Aether Architect is a first mobile game rather than a finished product — the build is playable, the world is real, and the systems underneath are the point.
